title: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
answer: Pathology detection and scan triage covers AI systems that examine medical images to flag suspected abnormalities and reorder radiology worklists by urgency. The work spans X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound, and includes findings such as lung nodules, intracranial hemorrhage, fractures and pneumothorax. These tools do not replace a radiologist's final read; they act as a second set of eyes and a prioritization layer. The goal is to reduce the time to diagnosis for urgent cases and to help manage high imaging volumes.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pathology detection and scan triage covers AI systems that examine medical images to flag suspected abnormalities and reorder radiology worklists by urgency. The work spans X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound, and includes findings such as lung nodules, intracranial hemorrhage, fractures and pneumothorax. These tools do not replace a radiologist's final read; they act as a second set of eyes and a prioritization layer. The goal is to reduce the time to diagnosis for urgent cases and to help manage high imaging volumes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically sit inside or alongside a hospital's picture archiving and communication system (PACS) and radiology information system (RIS). They receive DICOM studies, run inference on GPU-enabled servers either on premises or in a cloud environment, and return results through HL7 or FHIR messages to the worklist. Many deployments use a vendor-neutral archive or an orchestration layer to avoid disrupting existing workflows. Latency matters because triage results must arrive before the radiologist opens the next study.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most current tools use convolutional neural networks trained on large, labeled datasets of normal and abnormal scans. Detection models localize suspicious regions with bounding boxes or segmentation masks, while triage models assign a priority score based on the likelihood and severity of a finding. Training data is typically drawn from retrospective cohorts and annotated by radiologists, with careful splitting to avoid leakage between patients. After deployment, outputs are often reviewed against radiologist reports to monitor drift and false positive rates.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: These systems are generally regulated as medical devices and require evidence of safety and effectiveness before clinical use. Key risks include missed findings from false negatives, alert fatigue from false positives, and bias across patient populations or imaging equipment. The site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which underscores the legal exposure when triage or detection errors contribute to harm. Data provenance, patient consent for secondary use, and audit logs of model versions and decisions are central to compliance. Human oversight remains a requirement in most jurisdictions, with the radiologist retaining responsibility for the final interpretation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward foundation models that can handle multiple modalities and tasks from a single pretrained backbone, reducing the need for separate detectors per finding. Prospective clinical trials and real-world evidence are likely to replace retrospective validation as the standard for claims about triage benefit. Tighter integration with electronic health records may allow triage to weigh lab results and prior imaging, not just the current scan. Explainability and uncertainty estimates are expected to become more common so radiologists can judge when to trust a flag. Fully autonomous triage, where the AI reorders the worklist without human confirmation, remains a longer-term prospect.
